transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Recording: yes
Shared artifacts: bench spreadsheet (https://drive.google.com/open?id=hydra-bench-2026-09), routing policy playbook

[00:00] Ethan Rivera: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a sec; I know folks are on different timezones so appreciate it. I'm Ethan from Redwood, AE.
[00:17] Rachel Kim: hi Ethan, hi team, Rachel here, ready. Marcus and Tara are on as well.
[00:22] Marcus Doyle: yep, morning all.
[00:24] Tara Singh: hi, thanks.
[00:30] Ethan Rivera: quick agenda: we'll run through last week's bench numbers, a short routing playback of what we changed this sprint, discuss a weird tail latency bump we saw on the long-context tests, and then agree next steps. priya will share the SE notes.
[00:45] Priya Malhotra: thanks Ethan. um, so we pushed two changes into the lab — one was the continuous batching tweak to lower overhead for sub-128 token responses and the other was to enable prefix KV cache for repeat prompts. the baseline run numbers are in the sheet.
[01:02] Rachel Kim: can you remind us which baseline vendor you compared against? the sheet says CloudForge?
[01:08] Ethan Rivera: yes, CloudForgeAI — their default high-throughput endpoint, configured per their docs. we tried to mirror their concurrency and max tokens.
[01:20] Priya Malhotra: okay numbers first: for the 8k-context model variant A (the one you tried to match), mean latency at 32 concurrent connections was 180 ms per request on Redwood vs 240 ms on CloudForge; so about 25% mean improvement. throughput (tokens/sec aggregate) sustained at ~4.8k t/s on Redwood vs ~4.0k on CloudForge under that load.
[01:46] Marcus Doyle: that's mean numbers. what about p95 and p99? we care about tail — our UX is sensitive.
[01:53] Priya Malhotra: right, p95 was 420 ms on Redwood vs 380 ms on CloudForge — so we saw a tail regression there. p99 we saw some spikes up to 1.6s during a burst test but that's linked to long-running cache compaction on the node; we think it's a KV cache eviction interaction.
[02:14] Tara Singh: when you say cache eviction, do you mean KV cache for transformer key-value? does that mean tokens are being recomputed?
[02:21] Priya Malhotra: yeah so the implementation frees cached KV segments when memory pressure hits a threshold; afterwards there's a short penalty as KV is rebuilt. we have a mitigation path — smarter prefetch and a higher eviction watermark for the dedicated slot in the next run.
[02:37] Rachel Kim: earlier this week our engineers also saw occasional OOMs on CloudForge under the longer sequences; are you seeing any memory pressure anomalies on Redwood?
[02:46] Priya Malhotra: we saw one transient OOM during a stress test on model variant C at 16k context; that was due to a mis-set allocation across data-parallel groups in our lab config — fixed that and re-ran. not seeing persistent OOMs in steady-state.
[03:02] Ethan Rivera: to be explicit, for the Hydra pilot our recommended knob is to use Redwood's dedicated capacity with pre-warmed KV cache for the long-context flows, we saw better cost predictability that way. but hosted is fine if you want to start fast.
[03:18] Marcus Doyle: cost predictability matters — CloudForge's billing estimate jumped on us during a burst last month, so if your dedicated numbers are stable that's attractive. can you quantify cost delta?
[03:28] Priya Malhotra: ballpark with our current bench profile, per-1M tokens cost on Redwood dedicated profile was 18% lower than CloudForge hosted, but that depends heavily on batching and cache hit-rate; we included sensitivity rows in the sheet.
[03:45] Tara Singh: you mentioned batching — what's happening with the continuous batching tweak? are we losing long-tail QoE for some prompt shapes?
[03:52] Priya Malhotra: it's a tradeoff — continuous batching groups small requests to improve throughput and lowers mean latencies, but it can add micro-queueing for very low-latency single-token responses. our routing policy currently routes low-latency critical prompts to a low-queue path (smaller batch) and the rest to the high-throughput pool.
[04:08] Rachel Kim: can we see that routing policy? that would help our infra team mirror it.
[04:12] Ethan Rivera: yes, Priya just uploaded the playbook — link in the sheet. I'll post it in chat again.
[04:20] [00:04:25] Priya Malhotra: (screen share) so here's the routing playbook — we have weight-based routing: 70% -> high-throughput (larger batch, q4 quant), 30% -> low-latency (smaller batch, int8). we also have a fallback to a smaller model variant when latency exceeds 1s.
[04:41] Marcus Doyle: interesting. how do you measure quality when quantizing — did you run any exact-match or rouge-like tests?
[04:49] Priya Malhotra: yes, for the quant sweep we ran a side-by-side on 500 labeled prompts — average BLEU/ROUGE delta was negligible for q4, int8 showed a slight 0.9% drop on the most sensitive generative prompts. we can share the eval set anonymized.
[05:05] Rachel Kim: small drop could be fine. our main risk is hallucination increases. did you track hallucination or factuality?
[05:11] Priya Malhotra: we tracked a proxy metric — contradiction count against a ground truth for extractive tasks. no measurable regression for q4; int8 had a small uptick in spurious completions on the 12% of cases that are edge-cases.
[05:25] Tara Singh: on the numbers sheet I can see a row where Redwood throughput surpasses baseline but latency p95 is worse — can you walk through that specific test case?
[05:33] Priya Malhotra: sure, that's the long-context multi-turn conversation with prefix reuse enabled. because more keys are kept in cache for repeated prefixes we achieved much higher token/sec overall; however when the cache evicted during burst we saw the p95 jump since rebuild is synchronous for that request.
[05:51] Rachel Kim: ok makes sense. any proposed mitigation besides changing eviction thresholds?
[05:56] Priya Malhotra: yes — two things: pre-warm the cache for expected hot prefixes during ramp-up, and stagger eviction across nodes so there's no simultaneous mass eviction. also we can pin certain sessions to nodes for the session affinity cases.
[06:12] Marcus Doyle: pinning would simplify our guarantees but might reduce global utilization. what's the tradeoff?
[06:18] Priya Malhotra: exactly — pinning increases tail stability but lowers packing efficiency. we estimate a 6-8% throughput loss for aggressive pinning; depends on session churn.
[06:28] Ethan Rivera: quick interjection — we captured a rough simulation in the spreadsheet under the "routing simulation" tab; that should help quantify tradeoffs.
[06:36] [00:06:38] Rachel Kim: switching topics to security: can you confirm if Redwood can support our KMS/HSM + audit logs requirements in a private deployment?
[06:45] Logan Wu: yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations, and audit log forwarding. we provide syslog/ELK and also S3 export of event logs. we can share the SOC2 artifact and onboarding checklist after this call.
[06:58] Tara Singh: would we need a network hop for the KMS calls if we run in our VPC?
[07:04] Logan Wu: typically KMS calls go to your KMS endpoint inside your cloud region; we can do VPC peering or private link and keep traffic on the private network. Marcus we can run the network session to validate ports.
[07:15] Marcus Doyle: yes let's do that. I'll share our security contacts.
[07:18] Ethan Rivera: back to bench: Priya, you noted a one-off p99 spike during a multi-tenant burst. did you correlate to GC or compaction?
[07:25] Priya Malhotra: we correlated to a compaction cycle on the node that handles the KV eviction; there's a small lock that briefly blocks cache rebuilds — we've got a change to make compaction async and limit lock time. we'll test in the steady-state run.
[07:39] Rachel Kim: what's the plan for the steady-state run? time-box, traffic shape?
[07:44] Priya Malhotra: we'll run a 2-hour steady-state at target concurrency 48, with a mix of short (<=64 token) and long (4k-8k token) prompts matching your live distribution. we'll capture mean, p50, p95, p99, and token-level cost.
[07:56] Ethan Rivera: agreed. we'll also run a 30-minute burst test to simulate a small incident spike.
[08:03] Tara Singh: and you'll share the raw logs and trace IDs so our infra can cross-check?
[08:08] Priya Malhotra: yes, we'll provide traces, per-token breakdown, and the bench sheet with the raw samples.
[08:13] Rachel Kim: one more question — can we run the steady-state on dedicated slot(s) with pinning enabled as an experiment?
[08:20] Priya Malhotra: yes we can provision dedicated slots for the run; there may be a short lead to reserve them but we can do it for the next test.
[08:26] Ethan Rivera: recap real quick: Redwood runs steady-state 2hr test, Priya will adjust eviction watermark and run quant sweep results to update the sheet; Marcus shares VPC/KMS details; Ethan to send summary and playbook. Any other open items?
[08:41] Tara Singh: none from me.
[08:43] Marcus Doyle: all good.
[08:46] Rachel Kim: thanks everyone.
[08:48] Ethan Rivera: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the network session and post the bench run results.
[08:55] [End of recording]

Notes about transcript quality: auto-transcription occasionally mislabels proprietary names (e.g., q4 vs Q-4), which we've tried to correct in the sheet. There is some crosstalk and abbreviated sentences retained to keep authenticity.
